title: Largest Component Size by Common Factor
description:
# Largest Component Size by Common Factor

You are given an array `nums` of unique positive integers. Build an undirected graph where each value in `nums` is a node, and two nodes have an edge when their greatest common divisor is greater than `1`.

Return the size of the largest connected component. Connectivity is transitive: if `a` shares a factor with `b`, and `b` shares a factor with `c`, then all three values are in the same component even if `a` and `c` are coprime. The value `1` has no factor greater than `1`, so it is isolated unless it is the only node.

The greatest common divisor is the largest positive integer dividing both values. A connected group consists of all nodes reachable from each other along edges, and its size counts nodes.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [4,6,15,35]

**Output:** 4

**Explanation:** 4 shares factor 2 with 6; 6 shares factor 3 with 15; 15 shares factor 5 with 35. All four nodes are connected by a chain.

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [20,50,9,63]

**Output:** 2

## Example 3:

**Input:** nums = [2,3,6,7,4,12,21,39]

**Output:** 8

## Constraints:

* `1 <= nums.length <= 2 * 10^4`
* `1 <= nums[i] <= 10^5`
* All values in `nums` are unique.

solutions.name: Value-Factor Union Find
solutions.description:
## Approach

Create a disjoint-set over integer values from `0` to `max(nums)`. For each number, factor it by trial division and union the number with each distinct prime factor. After all unions, count only roots of the original numbers.

## Key Insight

A prime factor can act as a hub node. Connecting every number to its prime factors produces the same transitive components as connecting every pair of numbers with a common factor.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * sqrt(max))
- Space Complexity: O(max)

solutions.name: Prime Owner Index Union Find
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build the disjoint-set only over indices in `nums`. For each distinct prime factor of `nums[i]`, remember the first index that contained that prime. Later indices with the same prime are unioned with that owner.

## Key Insight

The factor value is only a connector; it does not need to be a DSU node. Mapping each prime to one representative index is enough to merge every number that contains that prime.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * sqrt(max))
- Space Complexity: O(n + distinctPrimeFactors)

solutions.name: SPF Sieve with Index Union
solutions.timeComplexity: O(max log log max + n log max)
solutions.description:
## Approach

Precompute the smallest prime factor for every value up to `max(nums)`. Then factor each number by repeatedly using the SPF table, and union indices that share the same prime factor.

## Key Insight

The expensive part of repeated trial division is rediscovering factors. An SPF table turns factorization of each value into a short walk through its prime factors.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(max log log max + n log max)
- Space Complexity: O(max + n)

solutions.name: Divisor Bucket Sieve Union
solutions.description:
## Approach

Map every value in `nums` to its index. For each possible factor from `2` to `max(nums)`, scan its multiples. All present multiples of the same factor are unioned together.

## Key Insight

Instead of factoring each number, enumerate factor buckets directly. Every bucket represents one common factor greater than `1`, so all numbers inside that bucket belong to the same component.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(max log max + n)
- Space Complexity: O(max + n)

solutions.name: Prime Factor Bipartite BFS
solutions.description:
## Approach

Factor every number into distinct prime factors. Build a map from each prime factor to all indices that contain it. Then run BFS over number indices, expanding through each unused prime-factor bucket once.

## Key Insight

The graph is naturally bipartite: number nodes connect to prime-factor nodes. Visiting each factor bucket once gives connected component sizes without using a disjoint-set.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * sqrt(max) + totalFactorEdges)
- Space Complexity: O(n + totalFactorEdges)
